name: bioawk
why: AWK extended with understanding of biological file formats, a charming domain-specific twist on an old Unix classic.

brief.what_it_is: Bioawk is a modified version of Brian Kernighan's awk that understands common bioinformatics file formats. It reads optionally gzip'ed BED, GFF, SAM, VCF, FASTA/FASTQ, and tab-delimited files with column names. With the -c option it names the fields for you, so you can write things like $POS or $name instead of counting columns. It also adds a few built-in functions (the README's examples use revcomp and and) and a -t flag for tab-delimited input and output. The README says that when none of the new features are used, it should behave the same as the original BWK awk.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as an extension of Kernighan's awk that adds support for several common biological data formats, so that field-based text processing works directly on those formats.
brief.how_it_works: With -c, bioawk replaces awk's line-reading module with one that parses FASTA and FASTQ and reads gzip'ed files through zlib. It then adds variables that name the fields, taken either from a named format (sam, vcf, bed, gff, fastx) or from the first line of the input when -c hdr is used. The -t option is shorthand for -F'\t' -v OFS="\t". The README notes that without -c, awk falls back to the original line reader and does not handle gzip input.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no install steps beyond the formula. Building from source needs a YACC-compatible parser generator such as Byacc or Bison, and zlib for gzip support. No accounts, runtimes, or configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: It stays a drop-in awk for everything except the opt-in -c mode, and it adds named columns for formats like VCF and SAM through the header line. Its built-ins, such as revcomp, mean a one-liner can do sequence work that would otherwise need a script.
brief.status: quiet. The GitHub releases page lists a single release, v1.0, marked Latest, and says the last change on that release was made on 2013-08-27. The README has no newer notes. I did not check the commit history directly.
brief.caveats: The README warns that the replacement line reader does not fully mimic the original, and that it may fail in corner cases, though the author says this has not happened yet. Without -c, gzip input is not supported. Several strings in the new reader are never freed, which valgrind reports as still reachable; the author says these are not really leaks. Building needs a YACC-compatible parser and zlib. I did not see a license in the fetched text.

judge.reason: It makes AWK operate directly on FASTA, SAM, and VCF with named fields and sequence functions—a useful, distinctive way to explore bioinformatics data.

entry.title: bioawk
entry.tldr: Brian Kernighan's awk taught to read FASTA, FASTQ, SAM, VCF, BED and GFF, so genome files can be queried by column name in one-liners.
entry.deeper_look:
Bioawk is a modified copy of the original BWK awk. Add `-c` and name a format, and it gives each field a name, so you write `$POS` or `$name` instead of counting columns. It also reads gzipped input directly and adds a few built-in functions, such as `revcomp` and `and`. The README says that when none of the new features are used, it should behave exactly like the original awk.

It exists because bioinformatics files are mostly line-oriented text, which is what awk was built for, but the column layouts are easy to forget. SAM has a flag field packed with bits, FASTQ spreads one record over four lines, and VCF has a header you have to skip. Bioawk puts that knowledge inside the language, so the one-liner stays a one-liner.

Under the hood, `-c` swaps awk's line reader for one that parses FASTA and FASTQ and reads gzip through zlib. Field names come from a built-in format (sam, vcf, bed, gff, fastx) or from the first line of the input with `-c hdr`. The idea behind it is that a classic tool can be extended for a domain by changing how it reads records, while the language stays the same. If you know awk, you already know most of it.

Pulls the unmapped reads out of a gzipped SAM file by testing a bit in the flag field.

entry.whats_unique: It remains a drop-in awk apart from the opt-in `-c` mode, and it can take column names from a header line. Built-ins like `revcomp` replace small scripts for sequence work.
entry.caveats: The last release, v1.0, dates from 2013. The README warns the replacement line reader may fail in corner cases, and gzip input only works with `-c`. You also need your own FASTA, SAM or VCF files to try it on.
